title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbooks
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview

This page defines Redwood Inference's SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs), error budget policy, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. It is a normative reference for service owners, on-call engineers, and product managers.

Goals
- Ensure clear, measurable SLOs tied to customer experience.
- Standardize error budget actions and escalation.
- Provide repeatable capacity planning guidance to avoid hard-to-recover outages.
- Maintain high-quality incident reviews and learning loops.
- Provide operational tooling and runbooks that minimize time-to-recovery (TTR).

Key definitions
- SLI (Service Level Indicator): The metric that measures user-facing reliability (e.g., request success rate, p95 latency).
- SLO (Service Level Objective): The target for an SLI over a rolling measurement window (e.g., 99.95% success over 30d).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO. The allowable fraction of failures before corrective actions are required.
- Burn rate: Speed at which the error budget is being consumed (error budget used per unit time).

SLO design principles
1) Customer-centred: Define SLIs that reflect user experience (latency, correctness, availability).
2) Measurable & observable: All SLIs must be collected by the platform observability stack (metrics/trace/logs).
3) Limited number: Each service should own 1 primary availability SLO and up to 2 critical secondary SLOs (latency, correctness).
4) Actionable: SLO violations should map to prescriptive actions (rate limiting, traffic shaping, rollbacks).
5) Time windows: Use a primary window of 30 days for long-term health and a short window of 7 days for near-term detection.

Required SLOs and example targets
- Every externally-facing service (API gateway, hosted inference endpoints, auth/identity) must publish at least:
  - Availability SLO (success rate, 4xx optionally excluded) over 30-day rolling window.
  - Latency SLO (p95 or p99) for critical request types over 7-day rolling window.

Example SLO table (canonical examples for common services):

| service | sli | slo | measurement window | owner |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| hosted-api.generations | request success rate (2xx) | 99.95% | 30d | platform-api-team |
| hosted-api.generations | p95 latency (inference) | < 500ms | 7d | platform-api-team |
| embeddings.service | request success rate | 99.9% | 30d | embeddings-team |
| routing.control-plane | control-plane API success | 99.99% | 30d | infra-routing-team |
| dedicated-gpu-pool | job admission latency p95 | < 2s | 7d | dedicated-ops |

Measurement and tooling
- All SLIs must be implemented as Prometheus/exemplar-backed metrics with a documented query and exporter.
- SLO dashboards live in Grafana under the team folder and include: SLI timeseries, SLO burn-down (error budget remaining), and alerting state.
- Measurement windows: maintain both 7d and 30d rolling calculations for each SLO.
- Service owners must add SLO queries and dashboard links to the service's confluence page.

Error budget policy and action ladder
- Error budget computation: error_budget_remaining = 1 - observed_error_rate_over_window.
- Burn rate = (error_rate_observed / error_budget) normalized to the SLO window. Use the standard methodology described in the SRE book.

Action ladder (automated + human steps):
1) Normal (error budget > 50%): continue normal operations, report in weekly reliability digest if trend upward.
2) Watch (50% >= error budget > 25%): enable rate limiting for low-priority routes, open a reliability ticket, notify product and infra owners.
3) Restrict (25% >= error budget > 0%): apply stricter traffic shaping and increase sampling for traces; on-call lead performs a manual traffic re-route if possible; schedule immediate capacity mitigation.
4) Exhausted (error budget <= 0%): stop feature rollouts; canary traffic rollback or freeze deploys for affected services; raise to Sev2+ incident and exec notification per incident process.

- All actions must be logged in the incident tracking system (Jira) with an explicit error budget ticket.

Burn rate thresholds (example values):
- If burn_rate > 4x (on 1d window) -> trigger immediate paging to on-call + open incident.
- If burn_rate > 2x (on 6h window) -> notify on-call and product.

Capacity planning standards
- Forecasting cadence: quarterly forecasts with monthly refreshes; on-call/ops to run capacity checks weekly during peak traffic seasons.
- Inputs: recent 90-day qps growth, model size and GPU memory profile, seq-length distribution, scheduled large events (customer launches), and buffer for burstiness.
- Headroom policy: maintain N+20% GPU headroom for production pools and scale target such that 95th percentile queuing latency remains < target SLO under forecasted peak load.
- Autoscaling: prefer reactive autoscaling for worker pools, but maintain a baseline reserved capacity for critical services (Dedicated/Private customers).

Capacity calculation example (simplified):
1) Measured avg tokens/sec per GPU (T) = 12k tokens/s (example).
2) Expected peak tokens/sec (P) = observed_peak_qps * avg_tokens_per_request.
3) Required GPUs = ceil((P * safety_factor) / T). Safety factor = 1.2 for baseline headroom.
4) Add maintenance spare of 1-2 GPUs per pool for fast replacement.

Reliability initiatives and investment process
- Reliability improvement proposals are submitted as short RFCs and tracked in the reliability initiatives board. Proposals should include: measured pain (SLOs, incident frequency), proposed change, expected impact on SLOs/cost, rollout plan, and owner.
- Prioritization: reliability work competes with feature work via quarterly planning; use error budget consumption and customer impact as primary signals.
- Examples of high-impact initiatives: model quantization for stable latency, KV-cache layer to reduce token cost, cross-region failover automation, and cold-start avoidance for private deployments.

Incident review standards (post-incident process)
1) Triage and severity assignment: initial triage within 30 minutes of paging; severity assigned by on-call lead.
2) Incident timeline: create incident ticket within 1 hour and post status updates every 30 minutes for Sev1.
3) Post-incident: severity debrief within 24 hours.
4) Postmortem: publish a blameless postmortem within 72 hours for Sev1 and within 7 days for Sev2. Postmortems must include:
   - Summary (what happened, impact, customer-facing symptom)
   - Timeline (minute-by-minute for the critical window)
   - Root cause(s) and contributing factors
   - Detection & mitigation steps taken, and their effectiveness
   - Action items (owner, due date, verification plan)
   - SLO / error-budget impact and whether the action ladder triggered

Postmortem template (use this format):
- Title
- Incident ID
- Severity
- Start / End timestamps
- Summary (2-3 sentences)
- Impact (customers, revenue, SLAs)
- Timeline (table or bullet timeline)
- Root cause analysis
- Corrective actions (short and long-term)
- Preventative actions (tests, instrumentation, runbook updates)
- Verification plan and success criteria
- Links to dashboards/logs/alerts

Operational tooling and observability standards
- Metrics: all services must expose request success, request latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), queue length, and resource utilization.
- Dashboards: canonical SLO dashboard per service, on-call home dashboard, and a global SLO health dashboard.
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry spans for request boundaries and model invocation; sample rate configurable per error budget state (higher sampling when burning).
- Logging: structured logs (JSON) with request_id and user_tenant_id for quick traceability.
- Alerting: alerts should be SRE-actionable and map directly to runbook steps. Avoid too many noisy alerts; use Prometheus alert thresholding plus inhibition rules.

Example Prometheus alert rule (availability):
alert: HighErrorRate
expr: |-
  (sum_over_time((1 - (rate(http_requests_total{job="hosted-api",code=~"2.."}[5m])))[1h:5m])
  / 3600) > 0.0005
for: 15m
labels:
  severity: page
annotations:
  summary: "High error rate on hosted-api ({{ $labels.job }})"
  runbook: "https://confluence.internal/redwood/eng-sre/runbooks#hosted-api-5xx-spike"

Runbooks (canonical templates)
- All runbooks must be concise, prescriptive, and tested annually via game-days. Keep the first actionable steps under 10 lines. Each runbook must include: owner, pager criteria, quick mitigation steps, full remediation steps, rollback instructions, and verification.

Runbook: Hosted API 5xx spike (quick runbook)
1) Confirm paging alert and open incident ticket.
2) Identify scope using query: top 10 routes by 5xx in the last 5m.
3) If a single route is responsible for >50% of errors -> apply rate limiter to that route or disable new feature flag.
4) If errors are across routes: check upstream model service (hosted-inference) and GPU pool health.
5) Check recent deploys: `git log --since="2h" --pretty=oneline` and coordinate rollback if deploy correlates.
6) If backend saturation: scale worker pool by X replicas (use autoscaler or manual scale command).
7) Communicate status to product and customer success.
8) After service stabilizes, capture timeline and create postmortem.

Runbook: GPU memory OOM / model OOM
1) Check Kube pod logs and node conditions; run `kubectl describe pod <pod>` and `journalctl -u nvidia-driver` as needed.
2) Identify model and request size; inspect recent sequences that correlate to OOM.
3) If single request caused OOM: block offending request pattern (rate-limit, reject requests > max_seq_len).
4) If OOMs are systemic: scale up pool with nodes with greater GPU memory or enable model quantization/partitioned execution.
5) If model change caused regression: rollback model version and open model-onboarding review.

On-call and rotation guidance
- Pager duty: three-week rotational on-call with primary and secondary. Each team maintains an on-call runbook page with escalation contacts and Slack channel.
- Handover: daily handover message posted to the team Slack channel with outstanding incidents and any maintenance windows.
- War room: for Sev1 incidents create a temporary war-room channel and add the on-call, incident commander, product owner, and senior engineer.

Maintenance and validation
- Game-days: run at least two game-days per team per year to validate runbooks, dashboards, and capacity plans.
- Runbook testing: perform synthetic failure tests for top 3 runbooks annually and publish results.
- SLO reviews: quarterly SLO review meetings to adjust targets, SLIs, and measurement windows based on customer needs and observed behavior.

Ownership and escalation matrix
- Service owner: responsible for defining SLIs/SLOs, dashboards, and runbooks.
- SRE/Platform: responsible for the global SLO dashboard, alerting primitives, and autoscaling primitives.
- On-call lead: incident severity decisions, immediate mitigations, and ensuring postmortem completion.

Change log and governance
- Major changes to SLOs or error budget policy require an RFC reviewed by SRE leads and product stakeholders.
- This document is reviewed annually by the eng-sre team.

Appendix: useful commands and links
- Grafana SLO folder: https://grafana.internal/redwood/slo
- Prometheus queries: documented on team dashboards; canonical examples appended to each service page.
- Example commands:
  - `kubectl scale deployment hosted-api --replicas=10 -n production`
  - `kubectl logs -f <pod> -n hosted-inference`
  - `promtool check rules /etc/prometheus/rules/*.yaml`

If a service owner has questions about implementing these standards, reach out to the eng-sre team (eng-sre@redwood.internal) or raise a ticket on the reliability initiatives board.
